Welcome to the course. We will work through each concept carefully, connect the
ideas step by step, and use practical examples to make technical topics easier
to understand. When we introduce a new method, focus first on the problem it
solves and why it is useful. For example, in machine learning, features are the
information we give the model, while the target is what we want it to predict.
Now consider a simple question: what changes when the data contains missing
values? We will think through the reason and then look at the code. In Python,
we can inspect the data, run one small step at a time, and explain what the
result means. The goal is to understand the logic, not simply memorize syntax.

slides.title: Start
slides.transcript: Welcome to Module 13, Introduction to Spark SQL. In earlier modules, we used PostgreSQL to learn relational thinking. In this module, we keep that same thinking, but we move the execution environment to Spark. Spark SQL lets us write familiar SQL while Spark plans and executes the work across distributed data. The key question is not only whether the query is correct. We also ask what data is scanned, what has to move across workers, and what one output row represents. Keep a real project in mind as we work through this section—for example, a lakehouse processing millions of web events across many files. The technical feature matters because it changes what questions we can answer reliably and how easily another analyst can understand our work. As you listen, try to connect each SQL or data concept to a decision you might need to defend later: what the data means, what one row represents, what can be missing, and what assumptions the transformation introduces.

slides.title: Same ideas, different environment
slides.transcript: Spark SQL does not erase the SQL ideas we already learned. Filters, joins, grouping, windows, NULL handling, and row grain still matter. What changes is the execution environment. In PostgreSQL, we usually think about one database engine managing tables and indexes. In Spark, the work may run across many workers and many data partitions. That means a correct query can still be expensive if it scans too much data or causes large shuffles. Connect this idea to a healthcare analytics platform processing large longitudinal event tables. Ask what could go wrong if the concept were misunderstood: could rows be duplicated, important records disappear, categories be interpreted incorrectly, or a report become difficult to reproduce? A strong analyst can explain both the SQL operation and the assumption behind it. After the example, summarize the idea in one plain-language sentence before moving on.

slides.title: Learning goals
slides.transcript: By the end of this module, you should be able to explain when distributed processing is useful, describe the basic Spark execution model, and understand how Spark SQL and DataFrames connect. You should also be able to reason about lakehouse tables, schema choices, Delta tables, query plans, partitions, and shuffles at an introductory level. The goal is practical understanding, not cluster administration. Keep a real project in mind as we work through this section—for example, a retail pipeline aggregating high-volume sales data across partitions. The technical feature matters because it changes what questions we can answer reliably and how easily another analyst can understand our work. As you listen, try to connect each SQL or data concept to a decision you might need to defend later: what the data means, what one row represents, what can be missing, and what assumptions the transformation introduces.

slides.title: Roadmap
slides.transcript: We will start by asking why a workload might need distributed processing. Then we will introduce the Spark execution model. After that, we will connect SQL and DataFrames, discuss lakehouse and Delta concepts, and practice familiar SQL patterns. The last part of the module focuses on query plans, partitions, shuffles, and project-style reasoning. Keep a real project in mind as we work through this section—for example, a lakehouse processing millions of web events across many files. The technical feature matters because it changes what questions we can answer reliably and how easily another analyst can understand our work. As you listen, try to connect each SQL or data concept to a decision you might need to defend later: what the data means, what one row represents, what can be missing, and what assumptions the transformation introduces.

slides.title: Spark is not just bigger PostgreSQL
slides.transcript: A common misunderstanding is to think of Spark as PostgreSQL but bigger. Spark is different. PostgreSQL is a database system with transactions, constraints, indexes, and stored tables. Spark is a distributed compute engine. It can query tables and files, but its strength is large-scale analytical processing. In many real architectures, a database and Spark work together rather than replacing each other. When reading the example, do not read punctuation one character at a time. Start with the purpose of the query, then identify the input rows, the operation being applied, and the shape of the expected output. In a real setting such as a healthcare analytics platform processing large longitudinal event tables, this habit makes code reviews much easier because you can explain what the query is supposed to guarantee before discussing syntax. After running it, inspect a few records manually and check that the result matches that explanation.

slides.title: When a database may be better
slides.transcript: Spark is not always the right tool. A conventional database may be better for transactional workloads, frequent small updates, low-latency point lookups, and strict relational constraints. If the data fits comfortably in the database and the query workload is already efficient, moving to Spark may add complexity without much benefit. Connect this idea to a retail pipeline aggregating high-volume sales data across partitions. Ask what could go wrong if the concept were misunderstood: could rows be duplicated, important records disappear, categories be interpreted incorrectly, or a report become difficult to reproduce? A strong analyst can explain both the SQL operation and the assumption behind it. After the example, summarize the idea in one plain-language sentence before moving on.

slides.title: When Spark may be better
slides.transcript: Spark becomes useful when data and computation benefit from being divided across workers. Large file-based transformations, broad scans, batch feature preparation, and analytical pipelines across different storage systems are common examples. The main benefit is parallelism, but parallelism also introduces new costs such as coordination and shuffling. Spark distributes work across multiple processes and often multiple machines. The driver coordinates the job, while executors perform tasks on partitions of the data. This architecture becomes valuable when the data or workload is too large for one machine or when a platform needs scalable parallel processing.

slides.title: Distributed vocabulary
slides.transcript: These four words appear often in Spark. A partition is a chunk of distributed data. A task is a unit of work that runs on an executor. A stage is a group of tasks that can run before a new exchange is needed. A shuffle is the movement of data across workers. Shuffles often matter for performance because they require network and disk work. Spark distributes work across multiple processes and often multiple machines. The driver coordinates the job, while executors perform tasks on partitions of the data. This architecture becomes valuable when the data or workload is too large for one machine or when a platform needs scalable parallel processing.

slides.title: Driver and executors
slides.transcript: A Spark application has a driver and executors. The driver coordinates the application and builds the plan. Executors run tasks on data partitions. A beginner-friendly way to think about this is that the driver organizes the work and the executors perform the work. We should avoid collecting huge data back to the driver because that can create memory problems. Spark distributes work across multiple processes and often multiple machines. The driver coordinates the job, while executors perform tasks on partitions of the data. This architecture becomes valuable when the data or workload is too large for one machine or when a platform needs scalable parallel processing.

slides.title: SQL to distributed plan
slides.transcript: Spark SQL does not execute your text directly in one simple step. It parses the SQL, resolves tables and columns, optimizes the logical plan, and creates a physical plan. The physical plan includes operators such as scans, filters, joins, aggregates, and exchanges. Exchanges often indicate data movement. When reading the example, do not read punctuation one character at a time. Start with the purpose of the query, then identify the input rows, the operation being applied, and the shape of the expected output. In a real setting such as a lakehouse processing millions of web events across many files, this habit makes code reviews much easier because you can explain what the query is supposed to guarantee before discussing syntax. After running it, inspect a few records manually and check that the result matches that explanation.

slides.title: Lazy evaluation
slides.transcript: Spark uses lazy evaluation for many operations. A transformation, such as selecting columns or filtering rows, usually adds to a plan. An action, such as show, count, collect, or writing a table, triggers execution. This gives Spark time to optimize the work before actually running tasks. Spark transformations are often lazy: they build a logical plan rather than immediately processing every row. An action triggers execution. That gives Spark an opportunity to optimize the plan. Develop the habit of reading EXPLAIN output and asking which operations cause scans, shuffles, sorts, or exchanges.

slides.title: Spark SQL and DataFrames
slides.transcript: Spark SQL and the DataFrame API are closely related. SQL expresses the logic with SQL syntax. The DataFrame API expresses transformations through code. Both can use Spark's structured execution engine. For students who already know SQL, Spark SQL is a natural entry point into distributed processing. slides.title: Temp views
slides.transcript: A common workflow is to load data into a DataFrame, register it as a temporary view, and then query it with SQL. The temporary view is not the same as a permanent database view from Module 12. It is usually session-scoped and useful inside notebooks or jobs. Spark DataFrames and Spark SQL are two interfaces to the same underlying engine. You can prepare data with DataFrame operations, register a temporary view, and query it with familiar SQL. Choose the interface that makes the transformation easiest to read and maintain.

slides.title: Lakehouse layers
slides.transcript: A lakehouse combines file storage with table-like access. Raw files may enter the lakehouse first. Curated outputs are often stored as Delta tables. Spark provides distributed compute over those data assets. Reports, notebooks, and models consume the prepared results. This layered thinking helps keep raw, cleaned, and analytical data separate. A lakehouse combines scalable file-based storage with table-management features. Delta-style tables add transaction logs, schema controls, and reliable table operations on top of object storage. Keep raw ingestion, cleaned data, and curated analytical tables conceptually separate so lineage remains clear.

slides.title: Delta tables
slides.transcript: Delta tables add table behavior on top of data files. They use a transaction log to track table changes and support more reliable operations than plain collections of files. For this course, the key idea is that Delta tables make lakehouse data easier to query and manage as tables. A lakehouse combines scalable file-based storage with table-management features. Delta-style tables add transaction logs, schema controls, and reliable table operations on top of object storage. Keep raw ingestion, cleaned data, and curated analytical tables conceptually separate so lineage remains clear.

slides.title: Raw files vs managed tables
slides.transcript: A raw file is flexible, but Spark may need to infer or be given the schema. A curated Delta table has a stronger table contract. For teaching, think of raw files as ingestion material and tables as reusable analytical assets. That is not an absolute rule, but it is a helpful workflow. A lakehouse combines scalable file-based storage with table-management features. Delta-style tables add transaction logs, schema controls, and reliable table operations on top of object storage. slides.title: Schema inference caution
slides.transcript: Schema inference is convenient for exploration. Spark can look at data and guess types. But inferred types can be wrong, especially for identifiers, dates, mixed values, or sparse columns. For production workflows and important assignments, an explicit schema is often safer because it documents the expected structure. Schema inference is convenient for exploration, but production pipelines benefit from explicit schemas. A single malformed file or unexpected type can change inference or force expensive extra scans. Defining types up front also documents expectations and catches defects earlier.

slides.transcript: The browser practice database is intentionally small. It includes sales, admissions, survey responses, and web events. These are not meant to be big-data examples. slides.transcript: This query filters sales before returning results. In Spark, filters can be especially important because they may reduce how much data needs to be processed. slides.transcript: This example uses a cross join with a filter only to demonstrate that joins can multiply rows. slides.title: EXPLAIN habit
slides.transcript: This browser example uses EXPLAIN to build the habit of inspecting a plan. Spark EXPLAIN output is different and usually more detailed, but the habit is the same. Do not guess what the engine is doing. Inspect the planned operators and look for scans, filters, joins, aggregates, sorts, and exchanges. slides.title: Partitions
slides.transcript: Partitions are central to Spark parallelism. A dataset is divided into pieces, and tasks process those pieces. Too few partitions can limit parallelism. Too many small partitions can create overhead. As a beginner, you do not need to tune every partition setting, but you should understand why partitioning affects performance. Partitions organize data so the engine can avoid reading files that cannot satisfy a filter. Good partition columns are commonly filtered and have manageable cardinality. Column pruning similarly avoids reading unused columns. Both optimizations reduce I/O before more expensive computation begins.

slides.title: Partition pruning
slides.transcript: Partition pruning means Spark can skip reading some partitions when a filter matches the partition layout. A date column can be useful if queries often filter by date range. A unique ID is usually a poor partition column because it can create many tiny partitions. Partition design should follow query patterns. Partitions organize data so the engine can avoid reading files that cannot satisfy a filter. Good partition columns are commonly filtered and have manageable cardinality. Column pruning similarly avoids reading unused columns. Both optimizations reduce I/O before more expensive computation begins.

slides.title: Column pruning
slides.transcript: Column pruning means the engine may read only needed columns, especially with columnar formats such as Parquet and Delta. This is one reason SELECT star can be costly in large analytical work. It may be fine during exploration, but production transformations should choose needed columns deliberately. Partitions organize data so the engine can avoid reading files that cannot satisfy a filter. Good partition columns are commonly filtered and have manageable cardinality. Column pruning similarly avoids reading unused columns. Both optimizations reduce I/O before more expensive computation begins.

slides.title: Shuffle
slides.transcript: A shuffle happens when data must be redistributed across workers. This often occurs for GROUP BY, ORDER BY, DISTINCT, and many joins. Shuffles are not always bad. Sometimes they are necessary. But they are important because they involve network and disk work. In Spark performance reasoning, always ask where shuffles occur. A shuffle moves data across executors so related keys end up together. GROUP BY, large joins, and global ORDER BY can trigger expensive shuffles. In distributed systems, moving data is often more costly than evaluating the SQL expression itself, so plan around data movement.

slides.title: Group by and shuffle
slides.transcript: When we group by product, Spark must bring rows with the same product together. If those rows are spread across partitions, the engine needs a shuffle. This is why aggregation is not just a mathematical step. In distributed execution, it also has a data-movement cost. A shuffle moves data across executors so related keys end up together. GROUP BY, large joins, and global ORDER BY can trigger expensive shuffles. In distributed systems, moving data is often more costly than evaluating the SQL expression itself, so plan around data movement.

slides.title: Join cost
slides.transcript: Spark has several join strategies. If one side is small, Spark may broadcast it to workers. If both sides are large, the data may need to be shuffled by join key. A practical habit is to filter rows and select needed columns before a large join, as long as doing so preserves the correct logic. A shuffle moves data across executors so related keys end up together. GROUP BY, large joins, and global ORDER BY can trigger expensive shuffles. In distributed systems, moving data is often more costly than evaluating the SQL expression itself, so plan around data movement.

slides.title: ORDER BY caution
slides.transcript: A global ORDER BY can be expensive in Spark because the entire result needs a coordinated order. That may be necessary for a final report. It is often unnecessary in intermediate transformations. Sort only when the order is part of the actual requirement. A shuffle moves data across executors so related keys end up together. slides.title: Windows in Spark SQL
slides.transcript: The window function concepts from Module 11 transfer to Spark SQL. PARTITION BY defines groups. ORDER BY defines sequence. LAG and LEAD provide previous and next values. Frames define running or moving calculations. In Spark, these are powerful, but they may also require sorting and data movement. slides.title: Readmission-style sequence
slides.transcript: This example uses LAG to compare an admission with the previous discharge for the same subject. The logic is the same kind of sequence analysis we used earlier. In Spark, this window query may require sorting within each subject partition. Run the query and inspect the gap column. Window functions work in Spark SQL much like in PostgreSQL, but they can require sorting and shuffling within partitions. Define the business partition and sequence carefully, then inspect the physical plan when the dataset is large. Correct logic comes first; distributed cost comes next.

slides.title: NULL semantics still matter
slides.transcript: Spark SQL still uses SQL-style NULL semantics. Distributed execution does not make NULL easier or less important. Missing values affect comparisons, filters, joins, and aggregates. slides.transcript: The assessment starter asks for one row per product and month. The browser version is already complete so you can run it and inspect the result. In a student assignment, you can remove part of the SELECT or GROUP BY and ask students to finish it. After running it, explain the output grain and why a Spark version may need a shuffle for the grouping keys. For this activity, make a prediction before you run anything. State what one output row should represent, which records you expect to remain, and what edge case is most likely to expose a mistake. Then run the SQL and compare the result with that prediction. If it does not match, debug the logic in small pieces instead of changing several clauses at once. This is the same habit you would use in a real analytics project: validate the meaning of the result, not only whether the statement executes.

slides.title: Object decision guide
slides.transcript: This decision guide helps you choose where work belongs. Transactional workflows often belong in a database. Large file transformations often fit Spark. Reusable lakehouse outputs often become Delta tables. Small dashboard queries may fit a database or SQL endpoint. Batch feature preparation may fit Spark. The best choice depends on workload, freshness, governance, and scale. Connect this idea to a retail pipeline aggregating high-volume sales data across partitions. Ask what could go wrong if the concept were misunderstood: could rows be duplicated, important records disappear, categories be interpreted incorrectly, or a report become difficult to reproduce? A strong analyst can explain both the SQL operation and the assumption behind it. After the example, summarize the idea in one plain-language sentence before moving on.

slides.title: Module 13 takeaways
slides.transcript: These are the main habits from Module 13. Keep the relational thinking you built earlier. Add distributed cost awareness. Use raw files, temporary views, and Delta tables deliberately. Inspect plans. Validate outputs. And match the tool to the workload instead of assuming Spark is always better. Do not treat this as a list to memorize. Try to explain each idea using one example from a project you understand. If you can describe when you would use the concept, what assumption it makes, and how you would validate the result, you are ready to apply it independently.

slides.title: Next: Module 14
slides.transcript: Module 14 is the final project. You will bring together the course skills: understanding data, preparing it, writing SQL, validating outputs, and communicating results. The Spark SQL ideas from this module give you one more option for thinking about analytical scale, but the core habits remain the same: know your data, state the grain, validate your work, and explain your decisions. As you move forward, keep the reasoning habits from this module. The next topic will add new SQL tools, but it still depends on understanding grain, missing values, and the meaning of each transformation.
